data.content_ref: inline:{"analogy":null,"claim":"Popper's preference for the better-corroborated theory is defensible on his own terms not as an inductive prediction of future success, but as a methodological rule for maximizing informational content and minimizing known error, accepting that this offers no guarantee against future falsification.","counterconditions":[{"case":"If preferring Theory A over B based on past tests logically necessitates assuming the future will resemble the past (Uniformity of Nature), then the distinction collapses into induction.","checker_spec":null,"eval":"observation"},{"case":"If Popper's concept of verisimilitude (truth-likeness) cannot be formally defined without logical contradiction (as per Tich\u00fd and Miller), then it cannot serve as the non-inductive bridge for action.","checker_spec":null,"eval":"observation"},{"case":"If acting on a theory inherently assigns a subjective probability to its future success, then the 'risk-minimization' strategy is just Bayesian updating in disguise.","checker_spec":null,"eval":"observation"}],"definitions":[],"derivation":[],"formalization_refs":[],"mechanism":"The mechanism distinguishes between 'rational expectation' (which implies induction) and 'rational choice' (which implies selecting the best-tested option as the most informative current state of knowledge). By treating corroboration as a historical report of severity passed rather than a probability score, the scientist chooses the theory that has withstood the strongest attempts at refutation. This choice is rational because it utilizes the full weight of critical discussion, whereas ignoring corroboration would be irrational dogmatism. The 'smuggling' of induction only occurs if one assumes the choice guarantees future truth; if the choice is merely the best available basis for action while remaining fallible, induction is avoided.","premises":[],"schema":"deepreason-reasoning-envelope-v1","scope":{"covers":[],"excludes":[]},"simulation_refs":[],"uncertainties":[]}
